mcqs.question: Which statement correctly compares hydrogen bonding with ordinary dipole‑dipole interactions?

options.A: Both are equally strong and non‑directional.
options.B: Hydrogen bonding is generally stronger and highly directional because it involves H attached to N, O or F.
options.C: Dipole‑dipole interactions require H attached to electronegative atoms, while hydrogen bonds do not.
options.D: Hydrogen bonds occur only in gases, whereas dipole‑dipole forces are limited to liquids.

mcqs.answer: Hydrogen bonding is generally stronger and highly directional because it involves H attached to N, O or F.
mcqs.explanation: Hydrogen bonds are stronger than ordinary dipole‑dipole forces because the hydrogen atom is very small and highly positively polarized when bonded to N, O or F, leading to a strong, directional attraction. Options A, C and D misstate the nature and occurrence of these forces.

mcqs.learning_point: Distinguish intermolecular and intramolecular hydrogen bonding
mcqs.question: Which of the following molecules exhibits intramolecular hydrogen bonding rather than intermolecular hydrogen bonding?
mcqs.explanation: In salicylic acid the –OH group and the carbonyl oxygen are ortho‑positioned, allowing the hydrogen of the –OH to form a hydrogen bond with the carbonyl oxygen within the same molecule (intramolecular). Water, ammonia and methanol can only form hydrogen bonds with other molecules (intermolecular).

mcqs.question: Hydrogen bonding in a substance most directly leads to which of the following observable physical property changes compared with a similar molecule that lacks hydrogen bonding?
mcqs.explanation: Hydrogen bonds increase the overall intermolecular attraction in a substance, requiring more energy to separate molecules; therefore the boiling point rises. The other options describe opposite trends that are not caused by hydrogen bonding.

mcqs.question: Which of the following compounds is capable of forming hydrogen bonds?
mcqs.explanation: Hydrogen bonding requires a hydrogen atom covalently attached to a highly electronegative atom (N, O, or F). Water meets this criterion (H‑O). CO₂, CH₄ and N₂ lack such H‑X bonds and therefore cannot form hydrogen bonds.

mcqs.question: Select the correct definition of a hydrogen bond.

options.A: An ionic attraction between a metal cation and a non‑metal anion.
options.B: A weak van der Waals interaction present in all molecules.
options.C: A strong, directional attraction between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to N, O or F and a lone‑pair bearing electronegative atom of another molecule or the same molecule.
options.D: A covalent bond formed by sharing of electrons between hydrogen and carbon.

mcqs.answer: A strong, directional attraction between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to N, O or F and a lone‑pair bearing electronegative atom of another molecule or the same molecule.
mcqs.explanation: Option C captures the essential features of hydrogen bonding: involvement of H attached to N, O, or F and attraction to a lone pair on another electronegative atom. Options A, B and D describe unrelated types of bonding.

mcqs.learning_point: Distinguish intermolecular and intramolecular hydrogen bonding
mcqs.question: A molecule of ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) can form hydrogen bonds. Are these bonds intermolecular or intramolecular?

options.A: Intramolecular, because the O–H group is within the same molecule.
options.B: Intermolecular, because the O–H hydrogen can interact with O atoms of neighboring molecules.
options.D: Neither, ethanol does not exhibit hydrogen bonding.

mcqs.answer: Intermolecular, because the O–H hydrogen can interact with O atoms of neighboring molecules.
mcqs.explanation: In ethanol the O–H group can donate a hydrogen bond to the oxygen of another ethanol molecule, which is an intermolecular interaction. There is no internal H‑bond donor‑acceptor pair within a single ethanol molecule, so option A and C are incorrect. Ethanol certainly exhibits hydrogen bonding, so D is wrong.

mcqs.question: Water (H₂O) and hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) are similar in size, but water has a much higher boiling point. Which of the following best explains this difference?

options.A: Water molecules are heavier than H₂S molecules.
options.B: Water can form extensive hydrogen bonding, whereas H₂S cannot.
options.C: H₂S has stronger dipole‑dipole interactions than water.
options.D: Water has a larger molecular volume leading to greater London dispersion forces.

mcqs.answer: Water can form extensive hydrogen bonding, whereas H₂S cannot.
mcqs.explanation: The presence of strong hydrogen bonds between water molecules dramatically raises its boiling point. H₂S lacks hydrogen bonding because sulfur is less electronegative, so only weak van der Waals forces act. Molecular weight and dispersion forces are not the dominant factors here, making options A and D incorrect, and dipole‑dipole interactions in H₂S are weaker than in water, so C is wrong.

mcqs.question: Consider three liquids at 1 atm: (i) ethanol, (ii) dimethyl ether (CH₃OCH₃), and (iii) propane (C₃H₈). Which liquid will have the highest boiling point and why?

options.A: Propane, because it has the greatest molecular mass.
options.B: Dimethyl ether, because it has a permanent dipole moment.
options.C: Ethanol, because it can engage in hydrogen bonding.
options.D: All have similar boiling points because they are all non‑polar.

mcqs.answer: Ethanol, because it can engage in hydrogen bonding.
mcqs.explanation: Ethanol contains an –OH group that can form hydrogen bonds, leading to a significantly higher boiling point than dimethyl ether (which only has dipole‑dipole forces) and propane (which relies solely on London dispersion forces). Hence option C is correct; the other statements ignore the dominant effect of hydrogen bonding.
